title: Only Spiritually Awakened People Experience These 5 Things (And Can't Explain Why)
fullText: Something strange is happening to you. You think about a friend you have not spoken to in months. And 20 minutes later, your phone lights up with their name. You walk into a bookstore with no particular plan, pull a random book off a shelf, and the first page you open to answers the exact question that has been eating at you for weeks. A song comes on the radio at the precise moment you need to hear it, and the lyrics hit so close that you have to pull your car over. You tell yourself it is a coincidence, but the coincidences keep stacking up and somewhere deep down you are starting to wonder if coincidence is even the right word anymore. [music] Here is what almost nobody will tell you about these moments. They are not random. They are not a glitch in your perception and they are definitely not a sign that you are losing your mind. According to one of the greatest psychological thinkers who ever lived, these experiences are actually evidence that your mind is growing into something bigger than it used to be. Carl Young spent over 60 years studying the deepest layers of the human psyche. He worked with thousands of patients across his career. [music] He filled notebooks, journals, and volumes of academic work trying to answer one central question. Why do certain people start experiencing reality in a way that feels fundamentally different from everyone around them? [music] Why do some people suddenly see patterns, feel things before they happen, hold contradictions without breaking, and dream dreams that feel more real than Monday morning? And what he found was not a diagnosis. It was a map. A detailed, specific, [music] repeatable map of what happens to a human being when consciousness expands beyond its ordinary limits. [music] Today we are going to walk through five of the most significant experiences on that map. These are not vague spiritual platitudes. These are psychological events with names with documented patterns and with very specific effects on the people who go through them. [music] If you have been quietly wondering whether something unusual is happening inside you, this video is going to give you a framework for understanding it. And if you have never experienced any of this, you are about to get a window into a dimension of human experience that most people never even know exists. Let us start at the very beginning. [music] Experience number one, reality starts talking back. Carl Young coined a term in the mid- 20th century that most people today have heard, but almost nobody actually understands. [snorts] That term is synchronicity. Most people think synchronicity just means a meaningful coincidence. [music] two things happening at the same time that feel connected even though there is no obvious cause linking them and on the surface that is accurate enough but Jung was pointing at something much deeper [music] than that surface definition what Jung actually described was a shift in the fundamental structure of how a person experiences reality proposed that there is an underlying field connecting all events all consciousness and all [music] matter called it the unus mundus which is Latin for the unified world and he suggested that most people move through life without ever perceiving this field. [music] It is broadcasting constantly but they are not tuned to the frequency. When someone begins what Jung called the individuation process [music] which is his term for the deep psychological work of becoming a fully realized human being something changes in how they receive information from the world. Synchronicities stop being rare surprises. They become a steady stream, almost a conversation. Here is what this actually looks like in practice. You have been wrestling with a major decision for weeks. [music] You cannot figure out which direction to go. You go for a walk to clear your head and you pass a stranger having a phone conversation and you only catch five words of what they are saying, but those five words are the exact answer you needed. [music] Or you are reading a novel completely for entertainment and a character says something that dismantles a false belief you have been carrying since childhood. Or you are sitting in traffic running late, [music] frustrated, and a billboard catches your eye with a message so specific to your life situation that you feel like someone put it there for you personally. [music] The first time something like this happens, you shrug it off. The 10th time, you start paying attention. [music] By the hundth time you realize you are not seeing patterns because you are projecting them. You are seeing patterns because the patterns are genuinely there. Jung was careful to distinguish this from superstition or paranoia. [music] He was not saying the universe is literally placing billboards for your benefit. He was saying that consciousness and the outer world are more deeply linked than ordinary thinking allows and that when your inner life reaches a certain level of development and honesty, this linkage becomes perceptible to you in ways it simply was not before. There is a practical dimension to this that is worth naming. [music] Synchronicities have a quality of only working when you are in alignment with what Young called the self, capital S, meaning your deepest authentic nature. When you are performing a version of yourself for other people, when you are suppressing what you really feel or want, when you are operating from fear rather than from genuine desire, the synchronicities go quiet. But when you are living close to your truth, when you are paying attention, [music] when you are honest with yourself, they come flooding in. Think of it like a compass. Most people are wandering without one. [music] The awakened person discovers they have a compass they did not know they were carrying. Experience number two. you stop needing to choose sides. This is the one that confuses the people around you most. Young identified something he called the transcendent function. [clears throat] And despite the dramatic name, what it describes is actually very practical. It is the psychological capacity to hold two opposing truths at the same time without needing to collapse them into one. Before this capacity develops, human beings operate largely in what Jung called eitheror consciousness. You are either optimistic or realistic. [music] You are either spiritual or rational. You either forgive someone or you hold them accountable. You either want to leave or you want to stay. [music] Life presents itself as a series of either or choices. And you navigate by picking one side and then defending your choice. Most conflicts in human life from arguments between friends to wars between nations are rooted in this eitheror architecture. My truth or yours. my [music] group or yours, progress or tradition, individual freedom or collective responsibility. The list goes on forever. [music] But something shifts in the awakened person. They develop what Young described as the capacity to hold opposites in suspension, to live inside the tension between two things without forcing a premature resolution. And out of that tension, something new emerges. Not a compromise, not a splitting of the difference, but a genuinely new understanding that could not have arrived any other way. Here is an example that might make this concrete. Think about grief. Ordinary grief is excruciating because the grieving person is in conflict. On one level, they feel the loss as a wound. On another [music] level, they may feel relief or peace or even a strange gratitude for what the relationship gave them. These two experiences feel contradictory and the ordinary mind tries to resolve the contradiction by choosing one. Either I am devastated or I am at [music] peace. Either I am angry or I am grateful. The person who has developed the transcendent function does not have to choose. They can feel both fully simultaneously without one canceling out the other. And that capacity does not make them more confused. It actually makes them more whole. This shows up in practical everyday life in ways you might not expect. Awakened people tend to make decisions that puzzle others because they are not operating from either or logic. They can deeply commit to something while simultaneously remaining genuinely open to being wrong about it. They can love someone and clearly see that person's flaws without the love being undermined. They can take a strong position in a conversation while authentically listening to the opposing argument. [music] From the outside, this can look like inconsistency. It is not. It is comprehensiveness. There is a cost to this capacity, though. Most social situations, most arguments, most political conversations, most workplace dynamics run on either or energy. They need you to pick a side. [music] They need you to be a true believer. And when you cannot or will not do that because you genuinely see the validity in the shadow in every position, you become difficult to use. You are not available for tribal recruitment. You cannot be reliably angry at the right targets on behalf of the group. This [music] makes you in Jung's phrase psychologically unemployable by systems that depend on black and white thinking which is isolating but it is also once you settle into it profoundly freeing. [music] Experience number three. Your dreams become a second life. Everyone dreams but not everyone has the kind of dreams we are about to describe. Jung made a distinction between ordinary dreams [music] and what he called big dreams. Ordinary dreams are the nightly processing of daily experience. Your brain filing things away, working through anxieties, replaying conversations with slight variations. These dreams may have meaning if you work with them carefully, but they are still in the family of ordinary psychological experience. Big dreams are categorically different. A big dream has a quality of weight and reality that you can feel the moment you wake from it. You do not forget it the way you forget ordinary dreams. You carry it with you for days, sometimes for the rest of your life. The colors are different. The atmosphere is different. The sense of significance is overwhelming and it is not something you choose to feel. [music] It is simply undeniable. Jung documented his own big dreams extensively. He described being initiated, instructed, and transformed by experiences that happened while he was asleep. He insisted that these were not metaphors or symbols to be analyzed from a distance. They were actual encounters with what he called the deeper layers of the psyche, layers that contain not just personal history, [music] but the accumulated wisdom and experience of the entire human species. This is where Young's concept of the collective unconscious becomes directly relevant. [music] Jung proposed that beneath your personal unconscious, the layer that holds your memories and your repressed feelings and your individual story, there is a deeper layer that is not personal at all. It is [music] shared. It is the same in every human being regardless of culture, history or geography. It contains the fundamental patterns of human experience. The hero, [music] the shadow, the great mother, the wise elder, the trickster, the lover. Jung called these patterns archetypes. [music] When someone is in the process of genuine psychological awakening, they begin to have access to this deeper layer in their dreams. They encounter figures and landscapes and initiatory experiences that do not belong to their personal history. They meet beings that feel ancient and authoritative. They undergo symbolic deaths and rebirths. They receive information that they could not have constructed from their conscious experience. And then there is the dimension of prophetic dreaming. Jung documented this carefully and he was honest about how strange it sounds from the outside. Some people at a certain stage of psychological development begin dreaming events before they happen. Not symbolically, [music] literally. A conversation that occurs word for word. A phone call with specific information. A crisis that unfolds exactly as it appeared in a dream weeks [music] before. Jung's explanation for this was not supernatural in the conventional sense. He pointed back to his concept of the unus mundus, the underlying unified field. If time is not as strictly linear as our everyday experience suggests, and quantum physics has been offering evidence in this direction for nearly a century, then it is not inconceivable that a sufficiently developed consciousness could, in the relaxed state of sleep, perceive events that have not yet unfolded in ordinary clock time. The challenge with prophetic dreaming is obvious. You cannot share it without sounding either delusional or arrogant. People who have not experienced it have no framework for taking it seriously. And the people who have experienced it tend to keep it quiet for exactly that reason. There is a loneliness in this that Young acknowledged openly. The dream life of the awakened person becomes richer and more significant than the waking lives of most people around them. They begin to look forward to sleep, not for rest, but for reunion with a dimension of reality that their ordinary days do not offer access [music] to. Experience number four, you become two things at once. This is probably the most difficult of the five experiences to put into language, but it is also the one that changes everything. Jung describes something he called the ego self- aaxis. To understand what this means in practice, you first need a clear picture of what he meant by these two terms. The ego in Jung's framework is your everyday personality. It is the you that has a name, a history, preferences, [music] ambitions, fears, and a face you recognize in the mirror every morning. [music] The ego is not bad. It is necessary. Without it, you could not function in the world. You could not hold a job or maintain relationships or navigate a grocery store. [music] The ego is real and it matters. But the ego is not all that you are. The self, capital S, is what Jung described as the totality of the psyche. [music] Everything you are, including the parts you are not consciously aware of, including the dimensions of your nature that extend beyond your personal history, including your connection to the collective human experience and possibly to something even larger than that. The self is not a concept you build up to. [music] It is what you already are at the deepest level. The ego is just the small piece of it that manages to fit through the narrow opening of ordinary awareness. [music] In most people, the ego operates as if it were the whole show. It is the boss, the CEO, the final word on everything. [music] Most people's entire experience of being a person is just the ego doing its thing day after day, completely unaware that it is more like a drop of water than an ocean. The awakening experience that Yung identified is the moment when the ego first becomes aware of the self. And this moment is, in his words, always a defeat for the ego. [music] Not because the ego is destroyed or diminished in any bad way, but because it suddenly has to come to terms with the fact that it is not the largest thing in the room. Here is what this feels like from the inside. You are having an ordinary conversation, maybe a tense one, something that would normally pull you all the way in. But alongside the normal experience of being in that conversation, there is another perspective running simultaneously. a [music] wider one, a quieter one, one that watches you having the conversation with a kind of compassionate detachment, able to see patterns in your own behavior and in the other person's behavior that the ego would normally be too involved to notice. You are present. You are real. You are genuinely engaged. [music] And at the same time, you are somehow watching the whole thing from a slight distance with a clarity that is not available to someone who is purely identified with their ego. This is not dissociation. Dissociation is a trauma response where you disconnect from experience to protect yourself. This is the opposite. This is being more present than before from more perspectives at once. Jung called this the relativization of the ego. The ego does not go away. It gets properly placed. It becomes one center of identity among several rather than the only center of identity there is. The practical effects of this are significant patterns that used to hijack you completely. Jealousy, defensiveness, old wounds being triggered, deep-seated fears. You can still feel all of these, but you watch them from a wider vantage point. And that wider view gives you a choice you did not have before. You can see the pattern activating in real time and decide whether or not to act from it. [music] One of the strange side effects described is what he called inflation. This is when the ego having caught a glimpse of the self tries to claim credit for what it has seen. The person goes from quietly experiencing expanded consciousness to loudly performing enlightenment. They start using their awakening as a new kind of status. They become insufferable in a different way than they were before. Jung was pretty [music] clear that the universe tends to respond to inflation with immediate and thorough humbling. [music] You will have a profound mystical insight on Thursday and say something genuinely stupid at a dinner party on Friday. You will feel completely free of your old patterns and then act them out more embarrassingly than ever in your most important relationship. This is not [music] failure. This is the system working correctly. The self does not allow the ego to capture it for long. Experience number five. Your personal life becomes a universal story. [music] This is the one that sounds the strangest and lands the deepest. Jung spent a significant portion of his career studying myths, not as bedtime stories or relics of primitive thinking, but as the most direct surviving evidence we have of the universal patterns built into the human psyche. He noticed that the same stories appear over and over again in cultures with no historical contact with each other. [music] The hero's journey, the descent into the underworld, the great flood, the death and resurrection, the terrible mother, the wise guide, the threshold guardian. [music] These stories are not coincidences of parallel invention. They are, in Jung's [music] view, the psyche's way of telling the truth about itself in symbolic form. These patterns are baked into the architecture of human experience, and they do not stay in mythology books. [music] They show up in every human life, including yours. Here is what this means in practice for someone who is awakening. You go through a period where everything falls apart. [music] Your career collapses or your marriage ends or you lose someone you love or your health fails. The ordinary interpretation is that this is just bad luck or a consequence of your choices or the random cruelty of an indifferent universe. The awakened interpretation does not replace [music] that. It adds a layer to it. You begin to recognize that what is happening to your specific life is also an instance of a universal pattern. [music] You are not just losing a job. You are going through the archetypal initiation of loss that strips away false identity and forces the growth of real identity. You are not just going through a divorce. [music] You are enacting the death and rebirth pattern that appears in every serious mythology the human race has ever produced. [music] This does not make the pain less real, but it places the pain in a context large enough to hold it. [music] Young called this living mythologically, and he was careful to explain that it is not a choice in the sense of deciding to interpret your life symbolically. It is an [music] experience. When the awakening is genuine, you simply start to perceive the mythological layer of your own life. It becomes visible the way 3D images in those old pictures become visible once your eyes learn how to see them. [music] Once you can see it, you cannot unsee it. There is a specific phenomenon that comes with this that Young called archetypal possession. This is when one of the universal patterns temporarily takes over a person's behavior and experience. You will recognize this in people around you once you know what to look for. [music] The person who lost their job and immediately becomes a reckless adventurer taking wild risks they would never normally take is being temporarily driven by the hero archetype. The person who after a significant loss becomes controlling and withholding is being visited by the shadow side of the great mother pattern. The person who turns into an insufferable know-it-all after reading three books on a subject is experiencing a mild inflation of the wise man archetype. Most people are not aware when this is happening to [music] them. The awakened person begins to catch it in real time, not just in others, in themselves. You will be in the middle of an argument with your partner and suddenly see that you are not just you and them having this specific argument. You are acting out the eternal tension between two principles that have been clashing since the first human beings tried to live together. And that recognition does not end the argument immediately, but it fundamentally changes what the argument is made of. It becomes possible to have the conflict without fully losing yourself inside it. Jung believed that this capacity, the ability to perceive the mythological and archetypal dimension of your own life, was one of the most important psychological developments available to a human being. Not because it makes you special, but because it gives you a relationship with your own suffering and your own joy that transcends the purely personal. Your life becomes in a genuine and non-grandio sense more than just your life. Let us bring this back to earth for a moment. If you are having these experiences, what should you do with them? First, take them seriously [music] without making them your entire identity. Young was very clear that spiritual experiences are not achievements to be [music] displayed. They are information to be integrated. The goal is not to become someone who talks constantly about your synchronicities or your big dreams or your expanded consciousness. The goal is to become someone who lives from the deeper knowledge these experiences provide. Second, expect the integration to be slow and messy. Jung did not describe awakening as a single dramatic event after which everything is clarity and peace. [music] He described it as an ongoing process, often uncomfortable, full of regression and shadow [music] and inflation and humbling that gradually builds a psyche capable of holding more of reality. more of your reality and more of the reality that connects you to every other human being who has ever lived. Third, find your people. Jung observed that the isolation of awakening is real and it is not going to fully go away. But there is a difference between being isolated because no one around you has language for what you are experiencing and being genuinely alone. There are people in the world who are living this same process. Some of them you will find in books in the margins of history in the documented lives of those who came before. Some of them you will find in person unexpectedly often through synchronicities that bring you together at exactly the right moment. Fourth, [music] stay humble and stay grounded. The worst outcome of any genuine spiritual or psychological opening is ego inflation. The conversion of authentic experience into personal superiority. [music] The more real your awakening, the more ordinary your daily life should look. Not because you suppress what you have experienced, but because genuine depth does not need to advertise itself. [music] And fifth, understand what Jung believed about why this matters beyond the personal. [music] Jung was not a casual thinker. He lived through two world wars. He watched the 20th century demonstrate in the most horrific possible ways what happens when large populations of unconscious people [music] follow unconscious leaders into unconscious patterns. He believed with a seriousness that is hard to overstate that the survival of the human race depended on enough individuals doing [music] the difficult interior work of becoming genuinely conscious. Not enlightened in some perfect transcendent sense. [music] conscious, aware of their shadows, capable of holding complexity, [music] able to see through the tribal eitheror narratives that have driven so much human destruction, grounded enough in their own depth [music] to resist manipulation by those who profit from mass unconsciousness. He believed that each person who genuinely undertakes this process adds something to what he called the sum total of consciousness available to humanity. that the invisible interior work of one awakening person ripples outward in ways they will never fully see or know. If you are experiencing what we have described today, you are not outside the human story. You are in a very specific way one of the people the human story is depending on to write its next chapter. That is not a burden to carry. It is a context that makes the difficulty worth it. Carl Young once wrote that the most terrifying thing is to accept oneself completely. Everything we have talked about today is downstream of that one act. [music] The synchronicities, the capacity for paradox, the vivid dreams, [music] the expanded identity, the mythological life, all of it becomes available in proportion to how deeply and honestly you are willing to look at who you actually are. Not the person you are performing for other people, [music] not the person you are trying to become. Not the person you were told you should be, the actual person with all the shadow and all the light. with all the contradiction and all the depth. That is where the awakening lives. It has always been there. [music] You are just learning to see it. If this resonates with something you are living right now, share this with someone who needs to hear it. And if you want to go deeper into Jung's map of the human psyche, the next video is waiting for you.
